title: Reading a Whisky Back Label | Craft Beer School
desc: How to read a whisky back label in India: ABV, age, cask, colouring, filtration, batch codes, excise marks and the statutory lines.
teaser: The front label sells. The back label tells you what is actually in the bottle, if you know where to look.
standfirst: Back labels carry the facts that the front label leaves out. Here is how to read them line by line and what is missing when a line is not there.
sections: The front sells, the back informs

The front label of a whisky is a piece of design. It carries the brand, the style and perhaps an age. The back label is where the producer puts the details that rules require and the details they choose to share. It is also where a lot of marketing language hides.

Reading it well takes a minute and tells you more than any shop description. Start with the numbers, then the words, then what is missing. Our guide to whisky label terms covers the vocabulary in more depth.

Three numbers matter most.

  • ABV: alcohol by volume, as a percentage. Scotch must be bottled at 40% ABV or more. Many craft whiskies sit at 46% or higher. Cask strength bottlings can go above 55%.
  • Volume: usually 750 ml in India, 700 ml in the UK and Europe and 750 ml in the US. Smaller sizes such as 375 ml and 180 ml are common in India.
  • Age statement: where given, it is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle, not an average. A 12 year old blend can contain older whisky but nothing younger.

No age statement is not a fault. It means the producer chose not to state one, often to blend more freely.
Cask words are useful but rarely complete

Many back labels describe the cask: matured in ex-bourbon barrels, finished in sherry casks, first fill, refill. These words are useful but rarely complete. A sherry cask could be one of several sherry styles. The label seldom gives the length of the finish.

Two other lines are worth looking for. Natural colour means no caramel colouring was added; Scotch rules allow plain caramel, often listed as E150a in some markets. Non-chill filtered means the whisky was not chilled and filtered to remove compounds that cause haze when cold. Both are usually stated by producers who chose not to do these things. If the label says nothing, assume either may have been done.
Indian back labels carry extra lines

A bottle sold in India carries several lines set by national and state rules. Rules vary by state and change often, so treat this as a general guide:

  • A food safety licence number and logo, under FSSAI rules.
  • A statutory health warning about alcohol and a warning against drinking and driving.
  • A maximum retail price printed for the state of sale.
  • A line such as for sale in a named state only, because excise duty is collected state by state.
  • In many states, an excise label, hologram or scannable code on the cap or bottle.

These lines tell you the bottle passed through the legal channel for that state. They tell you nothing about flavour.
What the words on Indian whisky mean

Indian rules on what may be called whisky differ from the Scotch rules. Many Indian whiskies blend malt spirit with neutral spirit. A back label may describe the product as blended with Scotch malts or Indian malt spirit without saying what share each makes up. A single malt from an Indian distillery is a different product, made only from malted barley at one distillery.

Words such as premium, reserve, rare and select are marketing. They have no legal definition. Read past them to the numbers and the production details.
A batch code helps you find a bottle again

Most bottles carry a printed or laser etched code, often on the glass near the base or on the back label. It identifies the batch or bottling line. Some producers print a bottling date openly. Others use a code only they can read.

Whisky does not mature once bottled, so the date does not make the whisky better or worse over time. It does help when a whisky changes between releases, especially one without an age statement. If you loved one bottle, note its code.
Words that sound official but are not

Some phrases look like legal categories but are marketing. Small batch, hand crafted and cask selected all sound precise. No rule fixes what any of them mean. Our guide to what small batch means shows how loosely one of them is used.

Other words do carry rules in their home markets. Single malt Scotch must be made from malted barley at one distillery in Scotland using pot stills. Straight bourbon must be aged at least two years in new charred oak. Those definitions apply to whisky sold under those names, so the words are worth more than a slogan.

When in doubt, trust numbers over adjectives.
Read one label before your next purchase

Take one bottle from your cupboard and read the back label from top to bottom. Write down the ABV, any age, the cask details and whether it mentions colouring or filtration. Then note what is not there.

Now taste the whisky with those facts in mind. Does a 46% ABV non-chill filtered bottling feel fuller in the mouth than a 40% one? Can you find the sherry the label promises? Matching what you read to what you taste is the start of trained tasting.
faqs: What does the age on a whisky label mean?
It is the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. Older whisky may be in the blend, but nothing younger.
The whisky was not chilled and filtered before bottling, so it keeps compounds that can make it slightly hazy when cold. Many drinkers find it fuller in texture.
Is caramel colouring allowed in whisky?
Scotch rules allow plain caramel colouring. Labels that say natural colour indicate none was added.
Why does my bottle say for sale in one state only?
Excise duty on alcohol in India is collected by each state, so bottles are labelled for the state where duty was paid.
